analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $17 over five years.
analysis.headline: The bill raised the minimum wage from $7.25 to $17 an hour, but was referred to the Senate labor committee and never received a vote in the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the federal minimum wage in steps to $9.50, then $11, $12.50, $14, $15.50, and finally $17 an hour over about five years. After that, the minimum would rise each year with the wage of the typical American worker. It would also phase out the separate lower wage for tipped workers, the lower teen hiring wage, and the program that lets employers pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum. The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced and stayed there; it never reached the Senate floor for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid the federal minimum of $7.25 an hour, who have not seen a raise since 2009, would get scheduled raises up to $17. Tipped workers would eventually be guaranteed the full minimum wage instead of the $2.13 tipped cash wage. Workers with disabilities paid under special certificates would move to full pay. Wages would then rise automatically with the median wage so the floor does not erode again.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in yearly steps: $9.50, $11, $12.50, $14, $15.50, and $17 an hour, with the first step taking effect two or three months after enactment.
After reaching $17, ties future increases to the growth in the median hourly wage of all employees, so the floor keeps pace with typical pay instead of freezing for years as it did after 2009.

Phases out the separate tipped minimum wage: tipped workers' cash wage steps up to $17 and the separate lower tipped wage is repealed, while guaranteeing workers the right to keep their tips and requiring employers to inform them of that right.

Phases out the subminimum youth wage and the program that allows employers to pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum, with a transition period and assistance for affected employers and workers; no new disability pay certificates could be issued after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay near the minimum wage would bear the higher labor costs: restaurants with tipped staff, retail, agriculture, child care, home care, and other low-wage industries. Some of the cost would likely pass to consumers in prices, and some employers might reduce hours or staffing; economists debate how large those effects would be, and small businesses and nonprofits would face the same increases.

drawbacks.text: Minimum-wage employers would face steep cost increases, with the wage more than doubling from $7.25 to $17 over five years, and those costs fall hardest on labor-intensive businesses like restaurants, small retailers, and care providers that cannot easily raise prices or automate.

The Congressional Budget Office and many economists have found that sizable federal minimum wage increases reduce employment among some low-wage workers even as they raise pay for most; the provided sources do not include a CBO score for this bill, so the size of that trade-off is not established in the record here.

A higher federal floor applies uniformly across the country, even where local living costs are much lower, which is a common objection to statewide national rates; no state or local carve-out appears in the bill text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of workers earning at or near $7.25, the direct gains are large and concrete: a raise schedule that more than doubles their wage floor and then keeps it from eroding. The real costs fall on employers and consumers, and a well-designed analysis would weigh the risk of lost hours or jobs for some workers against the raise for most. The strongest design criticism is that a single national rate is a blunt tool for a country with widely different local wages. The bill's path out of the 2009 freeze, indexing to the median wage, addresses the recurring problem that a raised minimum quietly falls behind inflation for years.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2023 and referred to the Senate labor committee the same day, and the committee never took it up; no vote was ever held before Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced S. 2488 on July 25, 2023 with 29 cosigning senators listed in the bill's introduction.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced; that referral is the last action recorded for the bill.
The bill had 31 cosponsors, all Democrats, and died in committee without a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay the federal minimum wage are better off because the bill died: their labor costs stay at the 2009 level of $7.25 an hour, and no increase was enacted. Workers earning the minimum gained nothing from the 118th Congress.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Raise the Wage Act of 2023 in the Senate, the fourth consecutive Congress in which he has sponsored a $15-plus minimum wage bill.

for.name: Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Patty Murray (chair of the Appropriations Committee) and Dick Durbin (party whip), but did not move it out of committee.

against.name: Bernie Sanders
against.what_they_did: As sponsor, sat on the committee that received the bill; no markup or vote was scheduled even though the sponsor had a seat there, and the bill died on the committee calendar.

against.name: Bernie Sanders
against.what_they_did: No majority emerged in the 118th Senate to bring the bill to the floor; with 31 Democrats and one Independent as supporters out of 100 senators, no vote was scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 31 cosponsors was a Democrat; no Republican signed on, and in the divided Senate the bill never advanced from committee.

industries.industry: Low-wage employers (restaurants, retail, agriculture, care work)
industries.note: A step from $7.25 to $17 over five years would more than double the wage floor these businesses must pay, raising labor costs for restaurants with tipped staff, small retailers, and care providers; some of that cost would pass to customers or show up as reduced hours or jobs.
The bill phases out the separate tipped minimum wage (currently $2.13 federally) and guarantees tipped workers the full minimum, directly increasing payrolls in restaurants and bars.

industries.industry: Employers of workers with disabilities under special certificates
industries.note: The bill ends subminimum pay for workers with disabilities over several years and bans new certificates, raising costs for sheltered workshops and disability employment providers while moving workers toward full pay.
